title: COP31 and Climate Action’s New Centers of Gravity | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Council of Councils roundup ahead of COP31 in Turkey: climate action is shifting from pledges to deployment driven by energy security and industrial policy, with solar far outpacing IEA forecasts and emissions near a plateau (on course to fall 0.5% with Hormuz flows stalled), but it deepens dependence on China while multilateralism, adaptation and geoengineering governance lag and disinformation is cast as the real constraint.

insights.claim: Total global solar capacity in 2025 was more than ten times its 2015 level and grew by more than four times what the International Energy Agency predicted in 2015.
insights.speaker: Alice C. Hill
insights.so_what: Official agency forecasts have systematically underestimated solar; discount IEA-style baselines when sizing clean-energy demand.
insights.quote: has grown by more than four times what the International Energy Agency predicted in 2015

insights.claim: Solar photovoltaics are expected to account for almost 80 percent of worldwide growth in renewable electricity capacity, and in 2025 solar PV met over one-quarter of global energy demand growth.
insights.speaker: Alice C. Hill
insights.so_what: Solar is the dominant marginal source of new power; supply chains, inverters and grid equipment tied to PV carry the volume.

insights.claim: Battery capacity additions rose by about 40 percent in 2025, alongside solar growth.
insights.speaker: Alice C. Hill
insights.so_what: Storage is scaling with solar; battery makers and storage integrators benefit from intermittency pairing.

insights.claim: Steep price declines have made solar the cheapest energy source in many places.
insights.speaker: Alice C. Hill
insights.so_what: Economics, not policy pledges, now drive adoption, making deployment more resilient to political reversals.

insights.claim: Global climate action is shifting from pledges to deployment, with energy security and industrial policy emerging as the new centers of gravity.
insights.speaker: Alice C. Hill
insights.so_what: Track industrial-policy and energy-security budgets rather than COP pledges as the real drivers of clean-tech demand.
insights.quote: climate action is shifting from pledges to deployment, with energy security and industrial policy emerging as new centers of gravity

themes.theme: Emissions trajectory amid AI demand and Hormuz disruption

insights.claim: Despite rising electricity demand from artificial intelligence and air-conditioning, global energy-related carbon emissions rose only about 0.4 percent last year.
insights.speaker: Alice C. Hill
insights.so_what: AI power demand is being met substantially by low-carbon supply; emissions growth is near a plateau.

insights.claim: With flows through the Strait of Hormuz stalled this year, global energy-related carbon emissions are on course to fall by 0.5 percent.
insights.speaker: Alice C. Hill
insights.so_what: A supply shock, not policy, is producing the emissions decline; the drop may reverse if Hormuz flows resume.
insights.quote: as flows through the Strait of Hormuz remain stalled, they are on course to drop by 0.5 percent

insights.claim: Nations responded to the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East by building out liquefied natural gas and restarting coal plants while simultaneously trying to cut dependence on imported fossil fuels.
insights.speaker: Alice C. Hill
insights.so_what: Energy-security shocks boost both LNG/coal and domestic renewables at once; a barbell rather than a clean switch.
insights.locator: Even as nations built out liquefied

insights.claim: Solar growth let some nations insulate themselves from fuel price volatility.
insights.speaker: Alice C. Hill
insights.so_what: Import-dependent economies have a hedging motive for solar that persists regardless of climate politics.
insights.locator: Growth in solar allowed some nations

themes.theme: China's clean-tech dominance vs US fossil pivot

insights.claim: China's industrial policy support for clean energy technology helped underwrite the global spread of solar.
insights.speaker: Alice C. Hill
insights.so_what: Global solar build-out is effectively a Chinese manufacturing export story.
insights.locator: The support provided by China’s industrial policy

insights.claim: The spread of solar has deepened global dependence on Chinese industry and technology, trading fuel-import risk for supply-chain dependence.
insights.speaker: Alice C. Hill
insights.so_what: Expect trade defenses, localization mandates and supply-chain diversification plays as states react to this new dependency.
insights.quote: But it also deepened dependence on Chinese industry and technology.
insights.locator: Growth in solar allowed some nations

insights.claim: China has doubled down on solar and other low-emissions technology while the United States shifted federal policy to favor fossil fuels under President Donald Trump.
insights.speaker: Alice C. Hill
insights.so_what: Policy divergence widens China's lead in clean-tech scale while US support concentrates on oil, gas and coal.
insights.locator: China itself doubled down on solar

themes.theme: Adaptation gap, El Niño and geoengineering

insights.claim: Meteorologists expect the 2026–27 El Niño to spread weather and temperature extremes across the globe, and the world is unprepared for such record-breaking events.
insights.speaker: Alice C. Hill
insights.so_what: Watch agricultural commodities, insurers/reinsurers and utilities for weather-driven volatility through 2027.
insights.quote: Meteorologists expect the 2026–27 El Niño to spread weather and temperature extremes across the globe.

insights.claim: The glacial collapse in Nepal and Tibet showed that the gap between climate adaptation and climate destruction is widening, making better monitoring and early-warning systems urgent.
insights.speaker: Alice C. Hill
insights.so_what: Early-warning and climate-monitoring infrastructure is an under-served spending area likely to attract public funds.

insights.claim: As adaptation lags, entrepreneurs, nations and scientists are increasingly embracing atmospheric interventions, yet no binding governance regime sets guardrails, so nations or private actors could deploy them with global effects.
insights.speaker: Alice C. Hill
insights.so_what: Unilateral geoengineering is an emerging geopolitical tail risk and a likely target of new multilateral regulation.
insights.quote: No binding governance regime sets guardrails, meaning nations or private actors could deploy them with global effects.
insights.locator: As climate impacts mount and adaptation

insights.claim: Solar's spread alone will not protect people from climate harm, and this year's record-setting temperatures should prod faster climate action at COP31 in Turkey.
insights.speaker: Alice C. Hill
insights.so_what: Expect COP31 messaging to pivot toward adaptation and harm reduction rather than only mitigation.
insights.locator: That solar energy is spreading widely

themes.theme: Multilateralism under strain, action moving outside negotiations

insights.claim: Climate multilateralism is in a tough spot, and the blame cannot be laid solely on the Trump administration: in Europe, parties critical of development assistance and of climate action's impact on competitiveness are gaining ground while budgets shift toward defense.
insights.speaker: Alex Benkenstein
insights.so_what: European climate finance and aid budgets face erosion from defense reprioritization; less concessional capital for Global South transitions.
insights.quote: The blame cannot all be laid at the door of the Trump administration.

insights.claim: Energy security has become the watchword in both the Global North and Global South, and it can justify either switching away from fossil fuel imports or continuing to exploit domestic fossil resources.
insights.speaker: Alex Benkenstein
insights.so_what: The same security narrative supports both renewables and domestic fossil production; resource-rich states will lean toward the latter.
insights.quote: a concept that can be used to justify switching away from fossil fuel imports, but equally to call for continued exploitation of domestic fossil fuel resources

insights.claim: In periods of threat and uncertainty, political time horizons shorten and circles of concern narrow, drowning out calls for ambitious long-term climate action.
insights.speaker: Alex Benkenstein
insights.so_what: Geopolitical stress structurally deprioritizes long-horizon climate commitments; expect weaker pledges at COP31.
insights.quote: In periods of threat and uncertainty, time horizons shorten and circles of concern narrow.
insights.locator: In periods of threat and uncertainty

insights.claim: The UNFCCC and Paris Agreement remain essential for questions markets cannot resolve, such as historical emissions responsibility and who finances adaptation and loss and damage.
insights.speaker: Alex Benkenstein
entities: UN Framework Convention on Climate Change
insights.so_what: Loss-and-damage and adaptation finance remain the contested core of negotiations; vulnerable states' trust hinges on them.
insights.locator: The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change

insights.claim: Climate action is increasingly driven by economic and strategic self-interest rather than altruism, with clean energy embraced as a path to affordable power, jobs, industrial opportunity and energy security.
insights.speaker: Alex Benkenstein
insights.so_what: Durable demand for clean energy rests on economics, making it less exposed to multilateral breakdowns.
insights.quote: Increasingly, altruism is not the main calculus in making the right climate decisions; it is simply the economically and strategically sensible thing to do.
insights.locator: Although the multilateral process remains central

insights.claim: The African Union's Climate Action Innovation Hub shows African entrepreneurs building climate solutions tied to resilience and jobs, but they need capital to scale.
insights.speaker: Alex Benkenstein
insights.so_what: A capital gap in African climate innovation is a potential opportunity for blended finance and venture investors.
insights.locator: The African Union’s Climate Action Innovation Hub

insights.claim: The failure to meet Paris targets is not a technology problem, since renewables are already cheaper than fossil fuels and proven incentive structures exist, but a political problem fanned by disinformation and polarization.
insights.speaker: Andrew Heffernan
insights.so_what: Climate policy risk is driven by political and information dynamics, not tech readiness; monitor polarization as a leading indicator.
insights.quote: is instead a political problem fanned by the flames of disinformation and polarization

insights.claim: The world will soon exceed the 1.5°C Paris target, and even the 2°C target seems likely to be surpassed.
insights.speaker: Andrew Heffernan
insights.so_what: Overshoot raises the value of adaptation, physical-risk pricing and resilience assets.

insights.claim: The Global Initiative for Information Integrity on Climate Change (GIIICC) funds journalism, research and public outreach and coordinates like-minded actors to improve access to accurate climate data worldwide.
insights.speaker: Andrew Heffernan
entities: Global Initiative for Information Integrity on Climate Change (GIIICC)
insights.so_what: Information-integrity initiatives are becoming a policy lever in climate governance alongside the UN Global Principles for Information Integrity.
insights.locator: The good news is that those issues

insights.claim: Efforts such as the GIIICC, the UN Global Principles for Information Integrity and the International Partnership for Information and Democracy are pivotal both for transborder problems like climate change and for sustaining a weakening liberal international order.
insights.speaker: Andrew Heffernan
entities: UN Global Principles for Information Integrity
International Partnership for Information and Democracy
insights.so_what: Frames climate governance as part of a broader fight over information ecosystems and the liberal order.
